The default method needs the force design rows of the full cell on the device: approximately \(N\cdot3\cdot L\cdot 8\) bytes (7 GB for 100k atoms at \(L\) = 3k), plus the posterior factors. The rows are built node by node and the uncertainty shape atom by atom, but all rows must fit in memory. On the Cantor benchmark (15k basis functions), a cell of 3.9k atoms needs approximately 6.4 GB on the GPU and 20 s on an A100-40GB. (aj eval --no-deriv-dtc is a different switch: it is for large cells with a GP model, not for --uq ard.)

--shape-path committee (on aj eval and aj calibrate; ACECalculator(..., shape_path="committee")) calculates the same shape without the design rows. The shape is a sum of squared forces of a linear ACE model with \(r\) coefficient vectors, one for each column of the shape factor. Thus the arrays are approximately \(N\cdot3\cdot r\cdot 8\) bytes, not \(N\cdot3\cdot L\cdot 8\). The values are the same to roundoff. Use it only for cells much larger than 3–4k atoms: at that size it is not faster and it needs more memory (approximately 13 GB).

In Python, shape_tau and shape_rank truncate the shape factor to a lower rank. The scales are fitted for the full rank. Thus a truncated shape keeps the ranking of atoms (Spearman 0.99 at rank 200 of 3680), but its coverage is much too low (0.54, not 0.90). Use it only to rank atoms.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
Revision 2 was validated on a CrMnFeCoNi (Cantor) alloy, labelled by the MACE-MH-1 foundation model. The test had 3680 training configurations, a 15k-function basis, and 34 large cells with cracks and dislocations that were not in training. Results:

  • The default (aniso, transfer exponent) met all coverage targets without target data. For example, the crack-tip coverage was 0.885, against a target of 0.88 or more.
  • Without the transfer exponent, the validation scale was too small (crack-tip coverage 0.81). The error is mostly approximation error, so a scale fitted on 80 % of the data underestimates the error of the model fitted on all the data.
  • Crack cells in training improved the crack tip (0.87–0.90), but not in all folds. The jackknife block size had no measurable effect.
  • The rank correlation between forces_std and the actual error was 0.29–0.38 on the large cells.

The validation tables and the acceptance report give all results, with confidence intervals.

A second study applies the method to silicon (with --ard-prior fixed), and compares it with Bayesian and POPS uncertainties. It also propagates the uncertainty to silicon properties, for example elastic constants and defect energies. The paper is J. R. Kermode, arXiv:2611.08678. Its code and results are on GitHub.

If you use --uq ard in published work, cite this paper. See Licence and citation.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Only forces are calibrated. The calculator gives no energy or virial uncertainty. Under --uq ard, the energy and virial variances in the aj fit prediction files are the untempered posterior variances. They are not calibrated, and they can be too small on small training sets. On the small Si test fixtures, the test energy errors are approximately 1–3 times the predicted std (rms z-score ≈ 2.5). Before you use energy variances, examine the energy rms_z in metrics.json.
  • Coverage is marginal in each group, for atoms that are exchangeable with the calibration configurations of the group. Only the support flag finds a shift that the groups do not resolve, for example a new phase or chemical order.
  • The uncertainty shape is a proxy. It measures how much the prediction at an atom changes with the training clusters in the fit. The method uses it as a proxy for where the approximation error is large. It ranks errors, but it does not predict them.
  • Posterior files from before revision 2 (schemas 1 and 2) give only the scalar forces_std. The other properties give an error that tells you to refit with --uq ard.

docs.title: Fit labels from a foundation model
docs.text: You can use a foundation model such as MACE-MPA-0 in place of DFT. Label your structures with it, and fit ACE to these labels. Tutorials 4, 5 and 8 use this method. This page shows each part.

docs.title: Fit labelled Atoms directly
docs.text:
load_fit_data accepts lists of ase.Atoms and also file paths. Thus labels that you calculate in Python do not need a file:

import jax
jax.config.update("jax_enable_x64", True)   # fitting needs float64

from ace_jax.basis.model import BasisSpec
from ace_jax.fit.pipeline import FitConfig, fit, load_fit_data, save_model

cfg = FitConfig(model=BasisSpec(order=3, max_degree=10, elements=("Si",)), arm="linear",
                m_per_species=0, e0="lsq", opt="lbfgs", r0=None, rungs=("map",),
                energy_key="energy", force_key="forces", stress_key="stress").validate()
data = load_fit_data(cfg, train=train_atoms, test=test_atoms)
res = fit(cfg, data)
save_model(res, "fit")

ace-jax looks for each label in this order:

  1. under its key in atoms.info (energy, virial, stress) or atoms.arrays (forces);
  2. in the energy, forces and stress results of the attached calculator. An example is the SinglePointCalculator that the ASE extxyz reader attaches.

If the results of the calculator are for a different structure, ace-jax gives an error. This occurs when you attach one calculator object to more than one structure: the calculator keeps only the results of the last structure.

docs.title: Stress or virial
docs.text:
ace-jax fits the virial. Calculators and DFT codes usually give the stress. Thus give the stress key, and the reader converts the stress: for a periodic cell, virial = −stress × volume.

  • If a configuration has a virial label, ace-jax uses that label.

  • A non-periodic configuration has no virial.

  • Python: FitConfig(stress_key="stress").

  • Command line: aj fit ... --stress-key stress, and the same on aj eval.

The stress can be a 3 × 3 matrix, a flat 9-vector or a Voigt 6-vector (xx, yy, zz, yz, xz, xy, the ASE order), in eV/Å³.

docs.title: Labelling with a foundation model
docs.text:
All ASE calculators can label structures. For MACE, install it in the same environment. If you do not have a GPU, use the CPU version of torch:

pip install mace-torch --extra-index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu

from ase.calculators.singlepoint import SinglePointCalculator
from mace.calculators import mace_mp

calc = mace_mp(model="medium-mpa-0", default_dtype="float64", device="cpu")
labelled = []
for a in structures:
    a = a.copy()
    a.calc = calc
    results = dict(energy=a.get_potential_energy(), forces=a.get_forces(), stress=a.get_stress())
    a.calc = SinglePointCalculator(a, **results)    # each structure keeps its own labels
    labelled.append(a)

MACE-MPA-0 and MACE-MP-0b3 have the MIT licence. Before you distribute labels from a different model, check the licence of that model.

If you publish work that uses labels from a MACE foundation model, cite I. Batatia et al., "A foundation model for atomistic materials chemistry", J. Chem. Phys. 163, 184110 (2025).

docs.title: The tutorials' labels
docs.text:
The tutorials include their labels. Thus, with their default settings, they do not need a labeller.

ace_jax.tutorials.labels.label(structures, model="mpa-0", cache=...) looks for each structure in a cache file that is part of the tutorials. The key is the content of the structure: numbers, cell, periodicity and wrapped positions, to 10⁻⁶. It runs MACE only for a structure that is not in the cache. This module is for the tutorials. It is not a stable API.

The cache files are in docs/user/tutorials/data/school/ in the repository. make_labels.py in that directory makes them again. Its docstring gives the commands.

docs.title: Least squares and the evidence
docs.text:
Two options help you compare fits with different basis sizes, as tutorial 5 does:

  • res.map.log_evidence is the log marginal likelihood of the training data at the fitted hyperparameters. You can compare it between bases fitted to the same data. A larger value shows that the data gives more support to the basis.
  • FitConfig(solver="lstsq") (aj fit --solver lstsq) is a weighted least squares fit. It has no prior, no evidence and no uncertainty (the predicted variances are zero). Its weights come from weights= (--weights). Use it only for teaching: a large basis overfits.

docs.title: Run MD with JAX-MD
docs.text:
JAX-MD is a molecular-dynamics library written in JAX. ace_jax.jaxmd gives an ace-jax model as JAX-MD energy and force functions. The neighbour list, the model and the integrator then run on the device in one compiled program.

The energy is the energy of ACECalculator with the same options. The two agree to roundoff.

Install

Install ace-jax with the jaxmd extra: pip install "ace-jax[jaxmd]". For a GPU, add the cuda extra: pip install "ace-jax[jaxmd,cuda]".

The jaxmd extra installs jax-md and its dependencies. These are approximately 40 packages, for example flax and pymatgen.

Enable float64 in Python

Fitting and radial learning need float64. The aj command enables float64 itself. In Python, enable float64 before any other code imports JAX:

import jax
jax.config.update("jax_enable_x64", True)

Alternatively, set JAX_ENABLE_X64=1 in the environment. ace-jax never changes the JAX precision setting itself. The JAX default is float32.

Many small cells

To run many small structures at the same time, see Evaluate many structures. Its neighbour lists also accept cells that are smaller than twice the cutoff.

docs.title: Run NVE
docs.text:
1. Make a JAX-MD space for the cell.
  2. Make the potential and the neighbour list with the cutoff of the model.
  3. Calculate the number of slots for each atom.
  4. Make the integrator and run it in a compiled loop.
import jax
jax.config.update("jax_enable_x64", True)
import jax.numpy as jnp
from ase.build import bulk
from jax_md import partition, simulate, space
from ace_jax import jaxmd

atoms = bulk("Si", "diamond", a=5.43, cubic=True).repeat(4)
box = jnp.asarray(atoms.cell.array.T)                  # JAX-MD: lattice vectors are columns
displacement, shift = space.periodic_general(box, fractional_coordinates=True)
R = jnp.asarray(atoms.get_scaled_positions())

rc = jaxmd.cutoff("fit/model.npz")
neighbor_fn = partition.neighbor_list(displacement, box, rc, dr_threshold=1.0,
                                      format=partition.Dense, fractional_coordinates=True)
nbrs = jaxmd.allocate(neighbor_fn, R)                   # not neighbor_fn.allocate
dt = 1.0 / 10.18                                         # 1 fs; time unit 10.18 fs (eV, A, amu)

def make(K):
    """The potential and a compiled chunk of 100 steps for K slots."""
    pot = jaxmd.potential("fit/model.npz", displacement, atoms.numbers, K=K)
    init, apply = simulate.nve(pot.force, shift, dt)

    @jax.jit
    def chunk(state, nbrs):
        def step(i, carry):
            state, nbrs = carry
            nbrs = nbrs.update(state.position)
            return apply(state, neighbor=nbrs), nbrs
        return jax.lax.fori_loop(0, 100, step, (state, nbrs))
    return pot, init, chunk

K = jaxmd.capacity(R, nbrs, displacement, rc + 1.0)     # slots for the cutoff + skin
pot, init, chunk = make(K)
state = init(jax.random.PRNGKey(0), R, mass=28.0855, kT=8.617e-5 * 300, neighbor=nbrs)

done, retries = 0, 0
while done < 10:
    new_state, new_nbrs = chunk(state, nbrs)
    if new_nbrs.did_buffer_overflow:                     # the list is too small
        nbrs = jaxmd.allocate(neighbor_fn, state.position)
    elif pot.overflow(new_state.position, new_nbrs) or not jnp.isfinite(new_state.position).all():
        K += 8                                           # an atom had more than K neighbours
        pot, _, chunk = make(K)
        state = state.set(force=pot.force(state.position, nbrs))   # the state keeps the last forces
    else:
        state, nbrs, done, retries = new_state, new_nbrs, done + 1, 0
        continue
    retries += 1                                         # run the same chunk again
    if retries > 3:
        raise RuntimeError("the chunk overflows again after 3 retries")

jaxmd.allocate replaces neighbor_fn.allocate. It avoids an error of JAX-MD with JAX 0.11 when a new list goes into a compiled function.

The forces are the gradient of the energy. They are in Cartesian coordinates, also with fractional positions. quantity.stress and the NPT integrators of JAX-MD take pot.energy.

Stress sign

JAX-MD gives the stress with the opposite sign to ASE.

Minimum image

The JAX-MD neighbour list uses the minimum image. Every width of the cell must be more than 2 × (cutoff + skin). For a smaller cell, JAX-MD misses neighbours and does not give an error. To check the cell, use jaxmd.min_image_ok(cell, rc + skin). For a smaller cell, use ACECalculator with ASE, or LAMMPS.

docs.title: Choose the slots
docs.text:
The model uses a fixed number of slots, K, for each atom. K sets the cost of the model.

  • K for the cutoff + skin (capacity(..., rc + skin)) is always sufficient between list builds.
  • K for the cutoff (capacity(..., rc)) is approximately 1.5 times faster. Atoms can then get more neighbours than K during the run.

If an atom has more neighbours than K, the energy and forces are NaN. The model never ignores a neighbour. After each chunk of steps, do these checks, as in the example above:

  • pot.overflow(R, nbrs) is true for an overflow at the last positions.
  • Non-finite positions show an overflow earlier in the chunk.

Then make the potential again with a larger K, and run the chunk again. The integrator state keeps the forces of the last step. Calculate them again with the new potential before you run the chunk, as in the example.

docs.title: Use the C++ kernel on a CPU
docs.text:
On a CPU, give ffi=True to potential:

pot = jaxmd.potential("model.npz", disp, atoms.numbers, ffi=True, K=K)

The C++ kernel then calculates the energy and the forces, on all cores. It reads a radial table, so the results agree with the JAX model to approximately 1e-8 of the largest force. On 32 cores, MD of Si cells of 216 to 1728 atoms is approximately 10 to 18 times faster.

Limits of the kernel

The kernel is for linear ACE models in float64 on a CPU. It gives first derivatives in the positions only: the stress works, second derivatives do not. ffi="auto" uses the kernel when it can, and the JAX model when it cannot.

docs.title: Memory
docs.text:
The model calculates the atoms in blocks of rows. Only one block at a time is in the memory of the device. potential selects the block size as export_lammps does for LAMMPS. Thus the memory is approximately the same as for a LAMMPS bundle.

To set the block size, give chunk= (rows) to potential. A larger block can be faster for a small model, but it uses more memory.

docs.title: Export a model to LAMMPS
docs.text:
ace-jax models run in LAMMPS with lammps-jax. lammps-jax gives pair_style jax/kk, a KOKKOS pair style that runs a compiled JAX program on the GPU. ace-jax writes the program and its metadata into one JSON bundle.

Install lammps-jax

  1. Install ace-jax with the lammps extra: pip install "ace-jax[lammps]". For a CPU run, also install "lammps-jax[cpu]". This gives the XLA CPU PJRT plugin (Linux x86_64 only).
  2. Build its LAMMPS plugin at the same version. Use the lammps-jax instructions.

The ace-jax CI tests the export with lammps-jax 0.2.1. The pair style runs on a GPU (KOKKOS with CUDA). It also runs on CPUs (KOKKOS with OpenMP) if you export with platform="cpu". The plugin refuses a bundle that was exported for the other platform.

docs.title: Export
docs.text:
The buffers of the bundle have fixed sizes. Calculate these sizes from the initial structure of the run:

import jax
jax.config.update("jax_enable_x64", True)
from ase.build import bulk
import ace_jax as aj
from ace_jax.export.lammps import export_lammps, neighbour_capacity

model, meta, _ = aj.load("fit/model.npz")                 # or a .yace
atoms = bulk("Si", "diamond", a=5.43, cubic=True).repeat(4)
cap = neighbour_capacity(atoms, meta["rcut"], skin=1.0)    # skin = the LAMMPS `neighbor` skin
export_lammps(model, meta, "si_bundle.json",
              max_atoms=cap["max_atoms"], max_edges=cap["max_edges"],
              k_dense=cap["k_dense"], max_neighbors=cap["max_neighbors"],
              max_owned=cap["max_owned"],
              type_elements=[14])                          # Z of LAMMPS types 1, 2, ...

type_elements maps LAMMPS atom types to elements. Type 1 is the first entry.

The aj export command does the same steps. It reads the initial structure from the first configuration of an extxyz file:

aj export --model fit/model.npz --out si_bundle.json --structure start.xyz \
    --skin 1.0 --type-elements Si

For the CPU backend, add --platform cpu. Add --procs px,py,pz to size the buffers for one MPI rank. Use the same grid in LAMMPS (processors px py pz). For a linear ACE model on CPUs, the export uses a C++ kernel in place of the XLA program. See CPU kernel. On a CUDA GPU, add --ffi to use a CUDA kernel. See GPU kernel.

export_lammps returns a dictionary, and also writes it in the bundle. Its ace_jax key records what was exported: the layout, the capacities, the use of the lean form and of splines, and the lammps-jax version.

In the LAMMPS input:

pair_style jax/kk <path to the PJRT GPU plugin>    # see the lammps-jax documentation
pair_coeff * * si_bundle.json

Run LAMMPS with KOKKOS on the GPU. For example: lmp -k on g 1 -sf kk -pk kokkos newton on neigh half -in in.lammps.

docs.title: Capacities
docs.text:
neighbour_capacity(atoms, rcut, skin=1.0, slots="skin", margin=8, list_headroom=0.5) returns all buffer sizes for a structure:

Key Meaning max_atoms owned plus ghost atoms (the ghost shell size comes from the face spacings of the cell, so it is also correct for triclinic cells) max_owned owned atoms (with 10% headroom); rows after it are never evaluated k_dense model neighbour slots per atom max_neighbors LAMMPS neighbour-list slots per atom (with 50% headroom: the list increases most when a structure is compressed) max_edges the packed edge buffer of the sparse and dense layouts

If a structure becomes too large for a buffer, the forces are never truncated without a message. The energy and forces become NaN, or LAMMPS stops the run. If this occurs, export again with sizes for the larger structure.

slots="cutoff" sizes the model slots only for pairs in the cutoff. On a five-component alloy, this is 1.2 to 1.4 times faster.

Warning

Use slots="cutoff" only for stable MD of a fitted model, where the coordination stays near the coordination of the initial structure.

docs.title: CPU kernel
docs.text:
On CPUs, the export uses a C++ kernel for linear ACE models. The kernel replaces the compiled JAX program. It runs one MPI rank per core, with one thread per rank. The export compiles the kernel the first time, and keeps it in a cache.

The export uses the kernel if all these conditions are true:

  • The model is a linear ACE model, in float64.
  • The bundle can use the matrix layout (--layout auto or matrix).
  • lammps-jax is version 0.2.1 or later.
  • The kernel is available: the ace-jax wheels for Linux and for macOS (arm64) include it. On other platforms, a C++17 compiler ($CXX, c++, g++ or clang++) is necessary.

If a condition is false, the export uses the XLA program. aj export prints the reason.

Environment for LAMMPS

A bundle with the kernel needs the variable LAMMPS_JAX_FFI_HANDLERS in LAMMPS. Without it, LAMMPS stops with an error that gives the variable. Export with --no-ffi to get a bundle that needs no variable.

lammps-jax version

The kernel needs the LAMMPS plugin of lammps-jax 0.2.1 or later. Earlier plugins register custom calls for CUDA only, so LAMMPS cannot find the kernel on the CPU. Build the plugin at the version of the Python package.

  1. Export with --platform cpu:

    aj export --model fit/model.npz --out si_bundle.json --structure start.xyz \
    --platform cpu --procs 8,4,4

    In Python, use export_lammps(..., platform="cpu").

  2. Set the variable that the command prints. It gives LAMMPS the kernel library:

    export LAMMPS_JAX_FFI_HANDLERS="ace_jax_direct=<library>:AceDirect"

  3. Run LAMMPS with newton on and one MPI rank per core:

    mpirun -np 128 lmp -k on t 1 -sf kk -pk kokkos newton on neigh half -in in.lammps

To get the variable on the machine that runs LAMMPS, use aj export --print-env si_bundle.json. If the library is not on that machine, the command compiles the kernel there.

Option Command line Python Use the kernel when possible (default) (no option) ffi="auto" Always use the kernel; stop with an error if it is not possible --ffi ffi=True Always use the XLA program --no-ffi ffi=False

The kernel tabulates the radial basis in r (radial_table=True). Energies agree with the XLA program to approximately 1e-12 relative. Forces agree to approximately 1e-8 of the largest force. The table is fine enough for an error of 1e-9 in the radial values. For most models it has 4000 intervals. The bundle records the kernel in ace_jax.ffi: the custom-call target, the library and the LAMMPS_JAX_FFI_HANDLERS value. If the export used the XLA program on a CPU, ace_jax.ffi_reason gives the reason.

For large models, --ffi-precision mixed (ffi_precision="mixed" in Python) is faster: 1.4 times for the silicon model o4d20 on 128 cores. The kernel then calculates the product basis in float32. It is off by default.

Mixed precision adds noise to the energy

Do not use min_style cg or other line-search minimisers with a mixed-precision bundle. Use min_style fire. See Mixed precision for the kernels.

The compiler flags are -O3 -march=native by default. They tune the kernel for the CPU of the machine that exports.

Login nodes and compute nodes

A kernel compiled with -march=native can fail on a different CPU type. Export on a node of the same type as the LAMMPS run. Or give generic flags, for example --ffi-flags="-O3 -march=x86-64-v3". To compile the kernel on a compute node before the export, use aj native --build.

  • The cache is ~/.cache/ace-jax/ffi. Set ACEJAX_FFI_CACHE to use a different directory.
  • Set ACEJAX_FFI_FLAGS to change the default flags.
  • Use the same jax version as the lammps-jax CPU plugin.

docs.title: GPU kernel
docs.text:
On a CUDA GPU, a CUDA kernel can replace the compiled JAX program. It is for linear ACE models, as the CPU kernel is. It supports categorical models with one or more species, and species-embedded (TrACE) models. The export compiles the kernel with nvcc the first time, and keeps it in the same cache.

CUDA compiler

The kernel needs nvcc. It finds $NVCC, nvcc on PATH, or $CUDA_HOME/bin/nvcc. On a cluster, load a CUDA module, for example module load CUDA/12.6.0. With an NVIDIA driver 580 or later, the cuda13 extra installs nvcc: pip install "ace-jax[cuda13]". The flags are -O3 -arch=sm_XY, for the GPU that JAX finds at the export. On a machine without a GPU, give the architecture, for example --ffi-flags="-O3 -arch=sm_80" for an A100.

  1. Export with --ffi. The platform is cuda by default:

    aj export --model fit/model.npz --out si_bundle.json --structure start.xyz --ffi

    In Python, use export_lammps(..., ffi=True).

  2. Set the variable that the command prints:

    export LAMMPS_JAX_FFI_HANDLERS="ace_jax_direct_gpu=<library>:AceDirectGpu"

  3. Run LAMMPS with newton on:

    lmp -k on g 1 -sf kk -pk kokkos newton on neigh half -in in.lammps

In float64, the requirements and the accuracy are the same as for the CPU kernel. On an A100, the kernel is 4.8 to 8.2 times faster than the compiled JAX program, for silicon models from o3d8 to o4d20 with 32,768 atoms.

The GPU kernel also runs float32 bundles. To export one, add --dtype float32. The kernel then calculates in float32, with the accuracy of the float32 XLA program. On a GPU with low float64 throughput, it is 2 to 4 times faster than in float64. On an A100, it is up to 1.7 times faster. The speed-up is largest for the largest models. See Learned radials and precision.

A float64 bundle can also use mixed precision (--ffi-precision mixed), as on the CPU. On a GPU it is slower than a float32 bundle. Its force error does not increase with the box size, because the positions stay float64. See Mixed precision for the kernels.

In Python, ACECalculator(path, ffi=True) uses the same kernel on a CUDA GPU. Add dtype="float32" for float32. BatchCalculator(..., ffi=True) also uses it. To compile the kernel before the first use, run aj native --build.

  • Set ACEJAX_FFI_GPU_FLAGS to change the default flags.
  • The source also compiles for AMD GPUs with hipcc (eval.ffi.build_gpu). It is not tested on AMD GPUs, and lammps-jax bundles do not run on AMD GPUs.

docs.title: Layouts
docs.text: Layout What it does When "auto" picks it matrix reads the LAMMPS neighbour list directly, copied only when LAMMPS rebuilds it; no per-step packing k_dense and max_neighbors given, the installed lammps-jax supports it, and a block fits in memory dense packs the edge buffer into per-atom slots every step k_dense given and matrix not chosen sparse an edge list no k_dense, or no dense block fits in memory

docs.title: GPU memory
docs.text:
The matrix and dense layouts evaluate the atoms in blocks of rows. One block sets the peak memory. export_lammps uses the largest block that fits in half of the GPU memory. It starts at 32768 rows and halves the block down to 1024 rows. If no block fits, layout="auto" uses sparse.

By default, export_lammps reads the memory of the GPU that does the export. If LAMMPS runs on a different GPU, give its memory:

export_lammps(model, meta, "si_bundle.json", ...,
              device_memory=30e9)                          # bytes JAX can use on the LAMMPS GPU

device_memory is the memory that JAX can use, not the total memory of the GPU. By default, JAX uses 75% of the GPU memory. For a 40 GB A100, use approximately 30e9. block_rows sets the block size directly.

The bundle records the block size as ace_jax.block_rows. It also records ace_jax.device_memory and ace_jax.dense_budget.

A LAMMPS plugin that is older than the lammps-jax Python package does not accept a matrix bundle. To correct this, build the plugin again at the version of the Python package, or export with layout="dense".

docs.title: Learned radials and precision
docs.text:
• lean=True (the default) exports the lean evaluation form, as the ASE calculator does. With spline_tol="auto", export_lammps first changes a learned radial to a spline at 1e-10; see Learn the radial basis.
  • dtype="float64" is the default. "float32" is faster and less accurate. On a GPU with low float64 throughput, a float32 bundle is 2 to 4.5 times faster. On an A100, it is 1.3 to 1.5 times faster. See Choose float64 or float32.
  • The float32 error depends on the model. Large coefficients that cancel make it larger.
  • precision_structure=atoms compares float32 with float64 on atoms. The bundle records the result as ace_jax.precision_check.
  • A warning occurs above 0.1 meV/atom of energy error or 1e-4 of relative force error. aj export --dtype float32 does this check on --structure.
  • ffi_precision="mixed" is for a float64 bundle with the kernel. The kernel then calculates the product basis in float32. The default is "float64".

docs.title: Large linear fits
docs.text:
This page shows how to fit a linear model with a large basis or a large dataset. It tells you which part of the fit takes the time, how to make a long fit resumable, and how to spread the fit over the nodes of a cluster.

Enable float64 in Python

Fitting and radial learning need float64. The aj command enables float64 itself. In Python, enable float64 before any other code imports JAX:

import jax
jax.config.update("jax_enable_x64", True)

Alternatively, set JAX_ENABLE_X64=1 in the environment. ace-jax never changes the JAX precision setting itself. The JAX default is float32.

docs.title: What takes the time
docs.text:
A linear fit has two long stages:

  1. Training statistics. ace-jax reads each batch of configurations, calculates its rows of the design matrix, and merges the rows into QR factors. The design matrix itself is never kept.
  2. MAP. ace-jax finds the hyperparameters that give the highest evidence. Each step factorises a matrix of size L × L, where L is the number of basis functions.

The training statistics take most of the time when the dataset is large. The force rows are the largest part, because each one needs the derivatives of all L basis functions.

The progress file progress.jsonl in the output directory records the time of each stage. The objective stage is the training statistics.

The table gives the measured rates for one dataset: 3600 configurations of 8 elements in 1904 batches, with L = approximately 21,000.

Stage Hardware Measured time Training statistics 4 nodes of 48 cores (Intel Xeon), one MPI rank each approximately 1700 batches per hour for each node (17 minutes in total) Merge of the 4 ranks, with checkpoints the same 4 nodes approximately 10 minutes MAP, --noise shared one node of 32 cores (mnf148) approximately 40 seconds for each step MAP, --noise per-quantity one node of 32 cores (mnf148) approximately 100 seconds for each step

Reading the dataset took approximately 70 seconds. Compiling the calculation took less than one minute. With --mpi, the rate for each node does not change, so N nodes take approximately 1/N of the time.

The MAP usually needs tens of steps. Thus, for this dataset the MAP takes approximately the same time as the training statistics. Its time does not decrease with more nodes. See Run the MAP as a second job.

The time of one MAP step increases as L³. At L = 47,000, one step takes approximately 11 times longer than at L = 21,000.

docs.title: Pack the configurations into batches
docs.text:
When the configurations have very different sizes, the default batches have much padding. Packed batches have less padding.

  1. Add --batch-pack on to aj fit.
  2. Compare the padding in the log line build_dataset: size-aware packing.

--batch-pack auto (the default) packs only when the default batches have more than twice the padding.

docs.title: Make a long fit resumable
docs.text:
A fit that stops, for example at a time limit, can continue from a checkpoint.

  1. Add --checkpoint DIR to aj fit.
  2. If the fit stops, run the same command again.

The fit then continues the training statistics from the last saved batch. If the training statistics are complete, the fit starts the MAP from the best hyperparameters found before.

--checkpoint-every MIN sets the time between two checkpoints. The default is 45 minutes.

Checkpoints are large

A checkpoint holds 8 L² bytes for each quantity (energy, force and virial). At L = 20,000 this is approximately 9 GB, and at L = 47,000 approximately 54 GB. A save can take several minutes. For a large basis, set --checkpoint-every to 120 minutes or more.

A checkpoint applies only to the same model, dataset and settings. ace-jax does not load a checkpoint of a different fit.

docs.title: Spread a fit over nodes with MPI
docs.text:
The training statistics use the memory bandwidth of a node more than its cores. Thus, more processes on one node give at most approximately 2 times the speed. More nodes give approximately N times the speed for N nodes.

aj fit --mpi divides the batches between MPI processes (ranks). Each rank calculates the QR factors of its batches. Then the ranks merge their factors on rank 0, which does the MAP and writes all outputs.

Only the training statistics are parallel

The MAP runs on rank 0 only. Its time does not decrease with more nodes. For a long MAP, use two jobs. See Run the MAP as a second job.

docs.title: Install the MPI extra
docs.text:
mpi4py must use the MPI library of your cluster.

  1. Load the MPI module of the cluster, for example module load OpenMPI.
  2. Make sure that mpicc is on your PATH.
  3. Install ace-jax with the mpi extra: pip install "ace-jax[mpi]".

On a computer without an MPI module, pip install mpich gives an MPI library for tests.

docs.title: Run the fit
docs.text:
Use one rank for each node. Give each rank all the cores of its node.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
#SBATCH --nodes=8
#SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=48
#SBATCH --time=48:00:00
module load GCC OpenMPI
export JAX_PLATFORMS=cpu OMP_NUM_THREADS=48 OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=48
mpirun -np "$SLURM_NTASKS" --map-by ppr:1:node --bind-to none \
    -x JAX_PLATFORMS -x OMP_NUM_THREADS -x OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS \
    aj fit --train train.xyz --test valid.xyz --order 3 --max-degree 4 \
    --batch-pack on --checkpoint ckpt --checkpoint-every 180 --mpi --out out
  1. Change the paths, the basis specification and the number of nodes.
  2. Submit the script with sbatch.
  3. Read the progress of each rank in the error log (qr stats rank ...).

Rank 0 writes the log, progress.jsonl and all outputs. The other ranks write only their progress lines to the error log.

Use a fast network

The ranks send their QR factors to rank 0 at the end of the training statistics: 8 L² bytes for each quantity. Use a cluster with a fast interconnect, for example InfiniBand.

With --checkpoint, each rank saves its own checkpoint in DIR. Run the same command with the same number of ranks to continue.

docs.title: Run the MAP as a second job
docs.text:
In one MPI job, the other nodes stay allocated but do no work while rank 0 does the MAP. Two jobs prevent this:

  1. A job on N nodes calculates the training statistics and stops.
  2. A job on one node reads the statistics from the checkpoint and does the MAP.

Do the steps that follow:

  1. In the MPI job script, add --stats-only to aj fit. Keep --checkpoint DIR.
  2. Write a second job script for one node. Use the same aj fit command, but remove --mpi and --stats-only. Do not use mpirun.
  3. Submit the MPI job: jobid=$(sbatch --parsable stats.sbatch).
  4. Submit the second job after it: sbatch --dependency=afterok:$jobid map.sbatch.
  5. Look for the log line checkpoint: QR statistics complete in the second job.
#!/usr/bin/env bash
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=48
#SBATCH --time=48:00:00
export JAX_PLATFORMS=cpu OMP_NUM_THREADS=48 OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=48
aj fit --train train.xyz --test valid.xyz --order 3 --max-degree 4 \
    --batch-pack on --checkpoint ckpt --out out

With --stats-only, rank 0 merges the factors of all ranks and saves them as one checkpoint file. The second job reads this file. It does not use the checkpoint files of the ranks.

The second job must use the same model, dataset and settings as the first job. If a setting is different, the second job does not find the checkpoint and calculates the training statistics again on one node.

The MAP needs much memory

The MAP needs approximately 90 L² bytes of memory. This is approximately 40 GB at L = 21,000 and approximately 200 GB at L = 47,000. For a large basis, use a large-memory node for the second job.

Disk space for the checkpoints

With --mpi, the checkpoint directory holds the checkpoint of each rank and the merged checkpoint. Each one is 24 L² bytes. When the second job has started, you can delete the files of the ranks (qrstats-*-r*of*.npz).

If the second job stops at its time limit, submit it again. It continues the MAP from the best hyperparameters found before.

docs.title: Check the result
docs.text: An MPI fit gives the same model as a fit on one node, to round-off. To check this on your cluster, fit a small dataset both ways and compare theta_map.json.

docs.title: Learn the radial basis
docs.text:
In a built basis, the radial functions are frozen: aj fit fits only the linear coefficients. The radial learner also optimises the radial mixing weights, by variable projection (VarPro). A validation gate then keeps the learned radials only if they predict better than the initial radials.

The output is a usual model.npz file. Thus all later steps (aj fit --model, ACECalculator, LAMMPS export) work without changes. Concepts explains the method. Tutorial 2 shows all the steps.

Radial learning needs float64. The aj command enables float64 itself.

Radial learning costs much more than a linear fit. Each L-BFGS step does one pass over the fit split, in batches. For example:

  • 26 two-atom silicon cells: approximately 2 minutes on a CPU;
  • production datasets of a few hundred cells: tens of minutes on a GPU.

docs.title: On the command line
docs.text:
aj fit --order 3 --max-degree 10 \
    --train train.xyz --test test.xyz \
    --e0 lsq --opt lbfgs \
    --learn-radial \
    --out fit

--learn-radial does these steps:

  1. It keeps a seeded validation set of the training configurations (--radial-val-frac, default 0.2).
  2. It learns the radials on the remaining configurations, and the validation set gates the result.
  3. It fits the coefficients on the full training set, as usual.

--learn-radial also works with --model, and with all final arms and UQ options. Its options are:

  • --radial-n-q 12: the number of polynomials for each radial. This option only increases the number. A model file that has more polynomials keeps them, and the fit log gives the number that is used;
  • --radial-steps 300: the number of optimiser iterations for each roughness weight;
  • --radial-reprofile-every 100: the interval, in iterations, at which the evidence hyperparameters are fitted again. Each new fit starts the optimiser again;
  • --radial-opt lbfgs: the optimiser. newton uses a trust-region Newton method with exact Hessian-vector products. One Newton iteration costs more than an L-BFGS iteration, but it usually makes more progress;
  • --radial-cg-iters 20: the maximum number of Hessian-vector products in one Newton iteration;
  • --radial-lam-grid 0,1e-2: the roughness weights. The gate selects from these weights and the initial radials.

The gate score is the sum of the squared validation errors of the energies and the forces, each divided by its noise variance. The learning objective uses the same weights.

The fit writes these files:

  • fit/radial_info.json: the selection of the gate, and the validation score of each candidate.
  • fit/model.npz: the learned radials. The file has a "learned" mark, so ace-jax changes the radials to splines at deployment (see below). If the gate keeps the initial radials, the file has no mark.
  • fit/fit.yaml: all settings of the run, including the radial options.
  • fit/radial_lam=<weight>.npz: the learned radials of each roughness weight (rnl_Wnlq). The fit writes each file when the learning for that weight stops, before the gate. These files stay if a later stage fails.

--learn-radial does not support species-embedded bases (--basis-embedding) at this time.

docs.title: Radial basis
docs.text:
--radial-basis sets the functions that make the tensor radials:

  • poly (the default): polynomials of a transformed distance, with an envelope, as in ACEpotentials.
  • sbessel: the simplified spherical Bessel functions of pacemaker (PACE), as functions of the distance. They are zero at the cutoff and after it.

--radial-basis is a basis option. It does not need --learn-radial. With --learn-radial, the learner changes the coefficients of the functions in the same way for the two bases.

Note

ace-jax does not change sbessel radials to splines at deployment. They stay exact, learned or not.

docs.title: In Python
docs.text:
import jax
jax.config.update("jax_enable_x64", True)

from ace_jax.basis.export import save_npz
from ace_jax.basis.model import BasisSpec, build_basis
from ace_jax.fit.pipeline import FitConfig, load_fit_data
from ace_jax.fit.pipeline.problem import build_problem
from ace_jax.fit.radial_learn import fit_radial, save_result
from ace_jax.fit.radial_model import rnl_degrees, to_analytic

save_npz("basis.npz", build_basis(BasisSpec(order=3, max_degree=10, elements=("Si",))))

# the linear problem on the fit split, with the validation split as its test set
cfg = FitConfig(model="basis.npz", arm="linear", m_per_species=0, e0="lsq", opt="lbfgs",
                r0=2.35, rungs=("map",)).validate()
d = load_fit_data(cfg, train="fit.xyz", test="val.xyz")
model, _ = to_analytic(d.model, 12)                      # widen to n_q = 12 polynomials
prob = build_problem(cfg, d).prob._replace(model=model)

W, info = fit_radial(prob, d.ds_train, d.ds_test, model.rnl_Wnlq,
                     lam_grid=(0.0, 1e-2),               # relative roughness weights to try
                     rough_weights=1.0 / (1.0 + rnl_degrees(d.meta)) ** 2,
                     steps=40, reprofile_every=20, log=print)
print(info["selected"], info["scores"])                  # the gate's choice and scores
save_result("learned", W, info, src_npz="basis.npz", model=model)   # learned/model.npz

Then fit the coefficients again on the full training set, and use the model as usual:

aj fit --model learned/model.npz --r0 2.35 \
    --train train.xyz --test test.xyz \
    --e0 lsq --opt lbfgs \
    --out fit_learned

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Argument Meaning to_analytic(model, n_q) the polynomial span of each radial. 12 is a small increase that optimises well. 30 is ill-conditioned and learns only small high-frequency changes steps, reprofile_every the maximum number of L-BFGS steps, and the interval at which the evidence hyperparameters are fitted again at the current radials lam_grid relative weights of a roughness penalty on the radials. Each value is a gate candidate (learned_lam=<value>) spec_grid, gap_grid optional relative weights of a spectral prior and a data-gap prior on the change of the radials. The gate also selects from these

If no learned candidate is better than the initial radials on the validation split, info["selected"] is "init". The saved model then has the initial radials and coefficients fitted for them, and it has no "learned" mark.

docs.title: With the research driver
docs.text:
bench/learn_radial/run.py in the repository does the same steps on one extxyz file, with a seeded fit/validation split. It is not part of the installed package.

python bench/learn_radial/run.py --model basis.npz --data train.xyz --out learned \
    --ntrain 26 --nval 13 --r0 2.35 --n-q 12 --steps 40 --lam-grid 0,1e-2

It writes learned/model.npz, the radial weights, the coefficients and a summary.json file with the gate scores.

Note

The research driver uses the E0 in the basis file. It does not fit E0.

docs.title: Deployment: spline speed
docs.text:
A learned radial is a polynomial mixture. Its evaluation is slower than the cubic splines of a stock model. Thus:

  1. The learner marks its output as learned (radial_learned in the metadata of the file).
  2. With the default spline_tol="auto", ACECalculator and export_lammps change the learned radials to cubic splines before evaluation, at a relative tolerance of 1e-10.
from ace_jax import ACECalculator

calc = ACECalculator("fit_learned/model.npz")
calc.splined        # {'spline_tol': 1e-10, 'radials': ['rnl'], 'n_intervals': {'rnl': ...}}
  • The splined model agrees with the exact model to approximately the tolerance, not to round-off. On the benchmark models, energies agree to approximately 1e-9 (relative), and forces to approximately 2e-8 of the largest force.
  • spline_tol=None never makes splines. A float (for example 1e-10) makes splines of all analytic radials, learned or not.
  • Bases built by ace-jax are analytic but not learned. Thus, by default, they stay exact.
  • The calculator keeps the splines in a cache, keyed on the content of the radials. Thus, if you replace only the coefficients (calc.model = ...), it does not make the splines again.
  • A learned-radial file written before the "learned" mark existed loads as not learned. To correct this, mark it with ace_jax.basis.export.mark_radial_learned("model.npz"), or give a float spline_tol.

docs.title: Fit a multi-element model
docs.text:
For more than one element, the command line does not change: aj fit builds the basis for all species in the training data.

On this page, you fit the five-component CrMnFeCoNi (Cantor) alloy. The training data is 40 small bulk cells, labelled by the MACE-MH-1 foundation model. Then you test the model in and out of distribution. The procedure takes approximately 4 minutes on a CPU. Tutorial 3 fits the same data in a notebook. It also compares the default categorical basis with species-embedding bases.

docs.title: The data
docs.text:
curl -LO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ACEsuit/ace-jax/main/docs/user/tutorials/data/cantor/cantor_train.xyz
curl -LO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ACEsuit/ace-jax/main/docs/user/tutorials/data/cantor/cantor_test.xyz
curl -LO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ACEsuit/ace-jax/main/docs/user/tutorials/data/cantor/cantor_vacancy.xyz
curl -LO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ACEsuit/ace-jax/main/docs/user/tutorials/data/cantor/cantor_compressed.xyz

The labels in these files are mace_energy, mace_force and mace_virial. Thus each command below gives these names with --energy-key, --force-key and --virial-key.

File Configs Contents cantor_train.xyz 40 bulk 32-atom fcc cells, strained and rattled cantor_test.xyz 30 the same distribution: in-distribution test cantor_vacancy.xyz 30 47-atom cells with one vacancy, unrelaxed: out of distribution cantor_compressed.xyz 30 compressed bulk: out of distribution

The data README tells how the subsets were made.

docs.title: Fit
docs.text:
aj fit --order 2 --max-degree 5 \
    --train cantor_train.xyz --test cantor_test.xyz --ood cantor_vacancy.xyz \
    --energy-key mace_energy --force-key mace_force --virial-key mace_virial \
    --e0 lsq --opt lbfgs \
    --out fit

basis Cr,Mn,Fe,Co,Ni order 2 max-degree 5 -> 206 B functions (elements from the data)
r0 2.500 A (mean bond length of the basis; pass --r0 to override)
...
RMSE, test (map)
-----------------------------------------------------------------
config type  configs  atoms  E (meV/atom)  F (eV/Å)  V (meV/atom)
-----------------------------------------------------------------
all               30   1200         25.60    0.1750        258.42
RMSE, ood (map)
-----------------------------------------------------------------
config type  configs  atoms  E (meV/atom)  F (eV/Å)  V (meV/atom)
-----------------------------------------------------------------
all               30   1122         30.32    0.1982        281.66

The files have no config_type, so each table has one row.

  • With five elements, the default categorical basis gives each species pair its own radial functions. Thus the basis becomes large quickly. Here, a small order and degree give 206 many-body functions for each species, and 1055 coefficients in total.
  • --basis-embedding <table.json> builds a species-embedded basis. In this basis, the species enter through a frozen element embedding, and --d-max sets the maximum channel width.
  • --ood adds a second test set. The fit writes its scores to metrics_ood.csv. The errors on the vacancy cells are only a little larger than on the bulk test set: a vacancy changes local environments that the bulk data already contains.

docs.title: Out of distribution: compression
docs.text:
aj eval --model fit/model.npz --data cantor_compressed.xyz \
    --energy-key mace_energy --force-key mace_force --virial-key mace_virial

RMSE, cantor_compressed.xyz vs fit/model.npz
-----------------------------------------------------------------
config type  configs  atoms  E (meV/atom)  F (eV/Å)  V (meV/atom)
-----------------------------------------------------------------
all               30   1152        179.24    0.9296       1097.39

The errors are several times larger than in distribution. In compressed cells, the neighbour distances are not in the training set. A linear model extrapolates to these distances without a warning. To correct this, add compressed cells to the training set.

docs.title: Load and write PACE .yace models
docs.text:
ace-jax reads pacemaker .yace potential files and evaluates them in JAX. It uses the same calculator, CLI and LAMMPS export as for its own models. The results agree with the ML-PACE C++ code, python-ace and LAMMPS.

If you use .yace models in published work, cite the PACE paper: Y. Lysogorskiy et al., npj Comput. Mater. 7, 97 (2021). For a model that pacemaker fitted, cite also A. Bochkarev et al., Phys. Rev. Materials 6, 013804 (2022). See Licence and citation.

docs.title: Evaluate a .yace
docs.text:
import jax
jax.config.update("jax_enable_x64", True)
from ace_jax import ACECalculator

atoms.calc = ACECalculator("model.yace")
atoms.get_potential_energy(); atoms.get_forces()

From the shell:

aj eval --model model.yace --data test.xyz --out predictions.xyz

docs.title: Supported features
docs.text:
Feature Supported radial basis ChebExpCos, ChebPow, ChebLinear, SBessel embedding FinnisSinclair, FinnisSinclairShiftedScaled inner cutoff density, distance, zbl

If a file uses a different feature, ace-jax gives an error when it loads the file. It does not evaluate the file incorrectly.

docs.title: Load, modify and write back
docs.text:
ace_jax.load returns a PACEModel, its metadata and the parsed file. The model is a JAX pytree of arrays. Thus you can change it with equinox tools. write_yace writes it to a file:

import ace_jax as aj
from ace_jax.eval import write_yace

pm, meta, spec = aj.load("model.yace")       # PACEModel, meta dict, parsed spec
write_yace(pm, "copy.yace", spec=spec)       # numbers from pm, layout from spec

write_yace takes the numeric values from the model. It takes all other data (the function layout, the element names, the file structure) from spec. Thus it never makes the basis layout again. If you write a model without changes, it gives the same results as the original.

The aj export command writes the same file:

aj export --model model.yace --out copy.yace

docs.title: Write an ACE model as a .yace file
docs.text:
write_yace also writes a linear ACE model (an .npz model) as a .yace file. The file gives the same energies, forces and stresses as the .npz model.

import ace_jax as aj
from ace_jax.eval import write_yace

model, meta, _ = aj.load("model.npz")         # a linear ACE model
info = write_yace(model, "model.yace")        # returns the sizes of the file
pm, meta, spec = aj.load("model.yace")        # ace-jax reads the file back

The aj export command writes the same file:

aj export --model model.npz --out model.yace

The file keeps the radial functions as tables of values. The table spacing is 0.001 Å. Set a different spacing with delta=. The cutoff must be a whole number of table spacings.

Warning

ML-PACE reads these tables only with its tabulated-radial addition. That addition is not yet in ML-PACE releases. Without it, LAMMPS refuses the file. ace-jax reads the file without it. For the status of the addition, see ML-PACE pull request 31.

Note

A model with more than one element gives a larger file. Each product of the model becomes one product for each combination of neighbour elements.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Use .yace models only for evaluation and export. aj fit and the radial learner need an ACE .npz model.
  • The return value of aj.load(path) depends on the file extension: .yace gives (PACEModel, meta, spec), .npz gives (ACEModel, meta, arrays).
  • For an SBessel radial with nradbase >= 12, ace-jax selects a matrix form at load time (PACEModel.sbessel_form == "matmul"). The values agree with the recurrence to round-off.

docs.title: Choose float64 or float32
docs.text:
ace-jax evaluates models in float64 or float32. float64 is the default and the reference. float32 can be faster, but it adds round-off error to energies and forces. This page tells you when float32 is faster, how to measure its error for your model, and which tasks can use it.

Fitting and radial learning always use float64.

Enable float64 in Python

Fitting and radial learning need float64. The aj command enables float64 itself. In Python, enable float64 before any other code imports JAX:

import jax
jax.config.update("jax_enable_x64", True)

Alternatively, set JAX_ENABLE_X64=1 in the environment. ace-jax never changes the JAX precision setting itself. The JAX default is float32.

docs.title: When float32 is faster
docs.text:
The speed gain depends on the float64 throughput of the GPU.

GPU float32 speed-up (silicon, LAMMPS, 32768 atoms) RTX A4500 (low float64 throughput) 2.1 to 4.5 times A100 (full float64 throughput) 1.3 to 1.5 times

Most workstation GPUs (RTX, L40) have low float64 throughput, as the RTX A4500 does. The gain is largest for small models and smallest for large models. On an A100, float64 is usually the better choice.

docs.title: Measure the float32 error of your model
docs.text:
The float32 error depends on the model more than on the code. Large coefficients that cancel make it larger. Thus, measure it for each model.

  1. Enable float64 (see above).
  2. Make structures that represent your task. Include the most distorted structures that the task visits, for example hot MD, defect cores or transition states.

  3. Compare float32 with float64 on each structure:

    import ace_jax as aj
from ace_jax.calc.precision import precision_check

model, meta, _ = aj.load("model.npz")
check = precision_check(model, meta, atoms)
print(check["dE_meV_atom"], check["dF_rel"], check["dF_max_meV_A"])

  4. Record the energy error per atom (dE_meV_atom), the relative force error (dF_rel) and the maximum force error (dF_max_meV_A).

aj export --dtype float32 --structure start.xyz does the same check on the initial structure of a LAMMPS run. A warning occurs above 0.1 meV/atom or a relative force error of 1e-4.

These are typical values for silicon models (linear ACE, order 4), from small to large:

error small model (degree 12 to 14) large model (degree 16 to 20) maximum force error 0.5 to 1.0 meV/Å 0.07 to 0.35 meV/Å relative force error 2e-4 to 4e-4 2e-5 to 1e-4 energy error 0.12 to 0.21 meV/atom 0.004 to 0.02 meV/atom

The errors on strongly distorted structures can be 5 to 25 times larger than these values.

docs.title: Tasks that can use float32
docs.text:
float32 is safe when the quantity that you need is much larger than the float32 error. Tasks that use forces are more tolerant than tasks that compare small energy differences.

task float32 MD with a thermostat: averages, radial distribution functions, diffusion safe NVE MD at a timestep of 1 fs or less safe geometry optimisation to a maximum force of approximately 3e-3 eV/Å or more, with a force-only optimiser safe properties of relaxed structures: elastic constants, defect and surface energies safe for well-conditioned models; measure first geometry optimisation to a maximum force of 1e-3 eV/Å or less; tight NEB or dimer searches caution NVE MD at 2 fs over long times caution small energy differences between large cells caution optimisers with an energy line search (L-BFGS or CG with Armijo or Wolfe tests) do not use finite differences of energies, free energy perturbation, thermodynamic integration do not use without a float64 check

docs.title: Geometry optimisation
docs.text:
Energy line searches fail in float32

The float32 energy noise is larger than the energy change along a short line search step. The Armijo and Wolfe tests then fail. Use an optimiser that uses only forces, for example ASE ODE12r.

import numpy as np
import ace_jax as aj
from ase.optimize import ODE12r

atoms.calc = aj.ACECalculator("model.npz", dtype=np.float32)
ODE12r(atoms).run(fmax=3e-3)

The optimiser cannot go below the float32 force error. Set fmax to approximately 3 times the maximum force error of your model, or larger.

docs.title: Molecular dynamics
docs.text:
In NVE MD of silicon (4096 and 32768 atoms, 10 to 40 ps, LAMMPS), float32 did not increase the energy drift at timesteps of 0.5 fs and 1 fs. It added noise of approximately 0.01 meV/atom to the total energy. This noise does not increase with time. At 2 fs, float32 possibly drifts by up to approximately 1 meV/atom per ns. A thermostat removes a drift of this size.

Large boxes in LAMMPS

A float32 LAMMPS bundle receives float32 atom positions. The round-off of the bond vectors thus increases with the box size. Measure the error in a box of the size that you use. The ASE calculator calculates bond vectors in float64, so this does not apply to it. With the kernel, mixed precision keeps float64 positions.

docs.title: Mixed precision for the kernels
docs.text:
The C++ kernel and the CUDA kernel for linear ACE have a mixed-precision mode. It is off by default. In this mode, the kernel calculates the product basis in float32. It calculates the bond vectors, the radial basis, the spherical harmonics and the sums over neighbours in float64. Positions, energies and forces stay float64.

Mixed precision is faster only for large models, where the product basis uses most of the time:

model (silicon, linear ACE) CPU, LAMMPS, 128 cores A100, ASE calculator o4d20 (5,476 basis functions) 1.4 times 1.4 times o4d16 1.1 times 1.1 to 1.2 times o4d14 1.1 times no gain o4d12 and order 3 no gain no gain

The errors are those of float32 for the product basis. For the silicon model o4d20, the maximum force error is approximately 0.05 meV/Å, and the energy has noise of approximately 0.1 meV in a cell of 200 atoms. For o4d16, the maximum force error is approximately 0.2 meV/Å and the noise is 1 meV. The errors are larger for smaller models, as they are in float32. The smallest models also have an energy offset that is the same for each atom: approximately 0.6 meV for o3d8 and 0.2 meV for o3d10 in bulk silicon. With a force-only optimiser, mixed precision changed no property of o4d20 by more than 0.013 of its tolerance in the silicon benchmark.

Energy line searches fail in mixed precision

The energy noise is the same type as in float32. Optimisers with an energy line search (L-BFGS or CG with Armijo or Wolfe tests) can fail near a minimum. Use an optimiser that uses only forces, for example ASE ODE12r or FIRE, or min_style fire in LAMMPS. The table in Tasks that can use float32 applies to mixed precision also.

Use mixed precision in place of float32 in these conditions:

  • On a CPU. The C++ kernel has no float32 mode.
  • In LAMMPS on a GPU with a large box. A float32 bundle receives float32 positions, and its force error increases with the distance from the origin (0.05 meV/Å at the origin, 0.8 meV/Å at 1000 Å for o4d20). A mixed-precision bundle receives float64 positions, and its error does not change.

On a GPU, a float32 calculation is faster than mixed precision and has approximately the same force error in a small box.

To set mixed precision:

  • ASE: ACECalculator("model.npz", ffi=True, ffi_precision="mixed"). calc.ffi["precision"] then gives "mixed".
  • Batches: BatchCalculator(..., ffi=True, ffi_precision="mixed").
  • LAMMPS: aj export --ffi --ffi-precision mixed, or export_lammps(..., ffi=True, ffi_precision="mixed"). The bundle records it as ace_jax.ffi_precision.

Mixed precision needs the kernel and float64. It uses the same compiled kernel library as float64.

docs.title: Check a new task
docs.text:
1. Measure the float32 error of the model on structures of the task.
  2. Compare the force error with the force tolerance of the task. Examples are fmax, the NEB tolerance and the thermal forces.
  3. Multiply the energy error per atom by the number of atoms. Compare the result with the energy differences that you need.
  4. Do a small number of calculations again in float64. For statistical results, for example free energies, also do a short float64 run.
  5. Use float32 only if it is faster on your hardware.

docs.title: Set the precision
docs.text:
• ASE: ACECalculator("model.npz", dtype=np.float32). See ASE calculators.
  • LAMMPS: export_lammps(..., dtype="float32") or aj export --dtype float32. See LAMMPS export.
  • Mixed precision of the kernels: ffi_precision="mixed". See Mixed precision for the kernels.

docs.title: Reproducible fits
docs.text: An ace-jax fit is deterministic. The same inputs, settings and software on the same platform give the same model, bit for bit. This page tells you what to keep, so that you can repeat or audit a fit later.

docs.title: Keep the run file and the model
docs.text:
Each aj fit writes fit.yaml next to the model. The file contains all options, with their final values, and a provenance block:

provenance:
  ace_jax: 0.1.0
  coupling: {backend: ace-jax-coupling==0.2.0, ..., platform: Linux-x86_64}
  command: aj fit --order 3 --max-degree 10 ...
  created: '2026-10-01T16:57:00Z'

aj fit --config fit.yaml --out again repeats the run (see Run files). The run file gives the paths of its data files. Thus keep the data with the run file, or record the checksums of the data files.

The fitted model.npz is self-contained. It contains the basis, the radials and the coefficients. Thus, to evaluate it later, you do not need the run file or the data.

docs.title: Seeds
docs.text:
--seed (default 0) is the seed for two random operations:

  • the random radial weights of a built basis (with --radial-mode glorot_normal);
  • the train/test permutation of --data ... --ntrain/--ntest.

A fixed seed always gives the same basis and the same split.

docs.title: Pin the software
docs.text:
• Record the environment: pip freeze > requirements-fit.txt, or keep the uv.lock of a uv project. Different JAX and NumPy versions can change the last digits of a fit.
  • ace-jax keeps the coupling coefficients in a cache, one entry for each basis specification. Each entry records the version of the coupling library. Thus, after a library upgrade, ace-jax calculates the coefficients again and does not use old entries. With --no-coupling-cache, ace-jax always calculates them again.

docs.title: Precision and platforms
docs.text:
• aj fits in float64. In Python, enable float64 before the fit (jax.config.update("jax_enable_x64", True)). The fit needs float64, and the radial learner gives an error without it.
  • --row-precision float32 calculates the design rows in float32. On a GPU, it also calculates their QR factors in float32. The evidence, the hyperparameters and the coefficients stay in float64.
  • This option is for the linear arm with the QR solver.
  • The GP arm (--m-per-species more than 0) and radial learning (--learn-radial) do not support float32 rows yet. With them, aj fit gives an error.
  • On a GPU with low float64 throughput, the rows are approximately 3 times faster. A complete fit was approximately 1.6 times faster in our tests.
  • The RMSE changed by less than 1 % in our tests. The hyperparameters can change more than the predictions do. Thus, compare one float32 fit with a float64 fit before you use float32 for a new type of dataset.
  • --row-check refits the hyperparameters on statistics with added noise of the float32 size. It records the change of the training RMSE in map_convergence.json. A change of more than 10 % gives a warning.
  • The coupling coefficients are bit-identical on Linux aarch64 and macOS arm64. On x86_64, they agree to a few units in the last place. Thus fits on different platforms agree to round-off, not bit for bit.
  • The default ACECalculator evaluation (lean=True) is exact to round-off. At deployment, a learned radial becomes a spline (to 1e-10). This is an approximation. For the exact evaluation, use spline_tol=None.

docs.title: Sharing a basis
docs.text:
Save a basis to a file if you want to:

  • fit more than one dataset with exactly the same basis;
  • let a person fit on a platform that does not have the coupling library.

To do this, save the basis one time with aj basis ... --out basis.npz. Then use aj fit --model basis.npz. Coupling cache entries are self-describing files. You can also copy them into the cache directory of a different machine.

docs.title: Python API
docs.text:
This page gives the public Python interface, in groups by task. All other parts of ace_jax are internal. They can change between releases.

Enable float64 in Python

Fitting and radial learning need float64. The aj command enables float64 itself. In Python, enable float64 before any other code imports JAX:

import jax
jax.config.update("jax_enable_x64", True)

Alternatively, set JAX_ENABLE_X64=1 in the environment. ace-jax never changes the JAX precision setting itself. The JAX default is float32.

import ace_jax as aj
model, meta, arrays = aj.load("model.npz")      # an ACE model, its metadata, the raw arrays

docs.title: ace_jax.load
docs.text:
load(
    path,
    dtype=jnp.float64,
    a2b_sparse="auto",
    edge_a_kind="gather",
    fold=True,
)

Load a model. Caller controls dtype; nothing here touches jax.config, so f64 requires the caller to have enabled x64 first.

a2b_sparse selects how A2B is held and contracted. "auto" (default): sparse triplets only, no dense A2B, when at most A2B_SPARSE_MAX_DENSITY of it is nonzero (every ACE coupling: 0.025-1.9% occupied), with B and dB/dA by sorted segment_sums (with_a2b_sparse). A file that stores a dense A2B is converted. True / False force the sparse / dense form. The dense form at 5456 basis functions is 2.6 GB, and its Jacobian costs 2 n_B n_AA n_A flops per node.

edge_a_kind selects how the A-basis product is formed: "gather" (default, today's behaviour) or "matmul", an algebraically identical one-hot form whose adjoint is a matmul rather than a scatter. Which is faster depends on the backend, the dtype and the edge-buffer length -- see calibrate_edge_a, and do not guess from the platform.

fold (default True) folds the linear readout through A2B (see fold_readout); pass False to keep the B-materialising path, e.g. to measure the fold by difference. Descriptors are unaffected either way.

docs.title: ace_jax.calc.point.ACECalculator
docs.text:
ACECalculator(
    model,
    meta=None,
    cutoff=None,
    dtype=None,
    edge_a_kind="auto",
    layout="auto",
    skin=1.0,
    lean=True,
    spline_tol=AUTO,
    spline_intervals=None,
    radial_table=None,
    aa_dag="auto",
    posterior=None,
    forces_std_every_call=False,
    energy_reference="absolute",
    shape_path="rows",
    shape_tau=1.0,
    shape_rank=None,
    ffi=False,
    ffi_threads=0,
    ffi_precision="float64",
    **kw,
)

Bases: Calculator

ACECalculator("si_fitted.npz") is the intended form: cutoff, species and dtype all come from the file. A pre-loaded (model, meta) pair is still accepted, which is what the validation tests use.

edge_a_kind picks the A-basis form (see EdgeSiteModel.edge_a): "gather", "matmul", or "auto" (default), which calibrates both on the actual neighbour list once per power-of-two edge-count bucket and keeps the faster, using the gather below AUTO_MIN_EDGES edges. It does not apply to a pool-first model (PACE, uses_edge_a False), which is used as given and reports last_edge_a_kind None.

layout picks the neighbour layout: "sparse" (edge list), "dense" (padded (n, K) per-node blocks; A by a batched outer product), or "auto" (default): dense when the padding is efficient (see MIN_DENSE_FILL), else sparse. edge_a_kind applies to the sparse layout.

skin (A, default 1.0) is the Verlet skin of the dense layout (see calc.skin): the neighbour list is built for cutoff + skin and reused, one compiled step per call, until an atom has moved skin / 2 or the cell, pbc or species change. skin=0 rebuilds the list every call. last_timing["rebuilds"] counts the calls that built a neighbour list, and last_timing["nlist_s"] is this call's build time (0 on reuse).

lean (default True) evaluates energies, forces and stress with ace_jax.eval.model.lean(model): exact to roundoff, with the per-edge work the energy never reads removed (docs/dev/ace-vs-pace-gap.md). spline_tol="auto" (default) first splines a learned analytic tensor radial (radial_learned, set by the radial learner) at 1e-10 (to_spline). That is not roundoff: energies agree with lean=False to up to ~1e-9 relative and forces to up to ~2.3e-8 of max|F| on the benchmark models (docs/dev/learned-radial-splining.md). Other analytic models -- ACEpotentials ace_model exports, built bases -- stay exact; a float spline_tol (e.g. 1e-10) opts them in, None never splines. spline_intervals pins the grid. calc.splined (and last_timing["spline_tol"]) says what was splined, None when nothing was. The spline is cached on the radial's content, and its grid is bucketed, so radial swaps usually keep the compiled step. It is eval_model; model stays the model as given, and descriptors use it. A PACE or unfolded model is evaluated as given either way. Setting calc.model recomputes the lean form on the host (a device-to-host copy of the model's arrays): negligible for MD, but a per-step cost if the model is swapped every step.

radial_table (None, the default: off; True: sized to a 1e-9 value error, from 4000 intervals up; a float: that tolerance; an int: that many intervals) tabulates the evaluation model's radial stage in r (eval.model.with_radial_table, after lean; ACE: R_nl with its transform and envelope, and the pair radial; PACE: g_k), one cubic B-spline per species pair on [0.5 A, rcut], exactly zero beyond each pair's cutoff. A CPU speed-up (1.1-1.4x on one core), and an approximation: with True energies agree to ~1e-11 relative and forces to ~1e-8 of max|F| (tests/test_radial_table.py). Applies with lean=False too (to the model as given). calc.radial_table is the table's info (n_intervals, r_min, r_max, max_rel_err, max_rel_deriv_err), None when off; last_timing["radial_table"] its n_intervals. Cached on the radial's content, so a readout-only calc.model swap does not rebuild it.

aa_dag ("auto", the default; None: the chain form; "greedy" or "prefix") evaluates the product basis as a DAG of one multiply per monomial (eval.aa_dag.with_aa_dag, applied to the evaluation model last). Exact to roundoff; "prefix" keeps every AA monomial bitwise. "auto" takes "greedy" from eval.aa_dag.AUTO_MIN_CHAIN_MUL chain-form multiplies per site, where it is faster on CPU and GPU, and the chain form below (a tie; bitwise as before). calc.aa_dag is the mode used. ("cueq", NVIDIA cuequivariance, was removed: on a CUDA GPU, ffi=True is faster.)

ffi (False, the default: the JAX model; True; "auto"; a library path) evaluates energies, forces and stress with the kernel of eval.ffi (its AceEdges entry point, KernelModel) in place of the JAX evaluation model: the C++ kernel on the CPU backend, the CUDA one (AceEdgesGpu) on a CUDA GPU. Same neighbour lists (the dense layout, the skin list), with forces and the virial assembled by JAX from the kernel's dE/drij. It needs lean=True, a linear ACEModel (categorical or species embedding) and float64 (float32 too on a GPU), and turns the radial table on (radial_table=None -> True; energies ~1e-12 relative, forces ~1.5e-8 of max|F|). The kernel is compiled on first use (eval.ffi.library: a C++17 compiler, or nvcc -- a toolkit's, or the cuda13 extra's -- on a GPU; cached). True raises ValueError (or eval.ffi.FFIUnavailable) when it cannot run; "auto" then keeps the JAX model and calc.ffi_reason says why. calc.ffi is {"library", "threads", "platform"}, None when off. On the CPU, rows run in parallel on XLA's intra-op thread pool; ffi_threads > 0 caps the threads. ffi_precision="mixed" (off by default; a float64 model) runs the kernel's product basis in float32 and the rest in float64 (eval.ffi.kernel_inputs): faster for large models (o4d20: 1.6x on a CPU), forces within ~1e-5 eV/A, but the energy carries ~0.1 meV of noise in 200 atoms, so relax with an optimiser that uses forces only (FIRE, ODE12r), not an energy line search. The kernel differentiates in positions only: derivatives in the model's parameters, or second derivatives, need the JAX model (ffi=False; calc.model and eval_model there).

posterior (a posterior.npz from fit --uq ard, with model the matching model.npz FILE) adds the per-atom force uncertainty. For a revision-2 (schema-3) posterior, each atom has a 3x3 shape V -- the centred delete-one-cluster (PRESS) jackknife covariance of its force (--ard-variance kappa: phi A^-1 phi^T) -- and a Mondrian group g that selects the calibrated scales: forces_std = lam_rms[g] sqrt(tr V), (N,); forces_cov = lam_rms[g]^2 V, (N, 3, 3); forces_q, the conformal radius at the fit's coverage (q[g] sqrt(tr V / 3) iso, the ellipsoid's largest semi-axis aniso); forces_q_mahal = q[g] (aniso); forces_group = g; and forces_support (on request). Schema-1/2 posteriors serve only the scalar forces_std (kappa times the epistemic std, or lambda times an uncentred configuration-clustered sandwich std). Energy and stress carry no uncertainty. By default the uncertainty is computed only when requested (calc.get_property("forces_std", atoms) or any of the above, which reuses the cached E/F/stress): a design-row rebuild plus an L^2 solve per step is not a silent MD cost. forces_std_every_call=True adds it to every calculation. posterior= requires jax.config.update("jax_enable_x64", True) (RuntimeError otherwise).

shape_path picks how a schema-3 jackknife shape V is evaluated: "rows" (default) builds the whole cell's force design rows (N, 3, L) and contracts them with R; "committee" evaluates the forces of the r-output linear ACE with coefficients D^-1 R (fit.jackknife.committee_shape), equal to roundoff, in memory O(N r) instead of O(N L) and without the edge Jacobian. shape_tau < 1 truncates R to the smallest rank holding that fraction of its sum sigma^2, and shape_rank (an int) caps the rank, on either path -- an approximation whose ranking and coverage loss against rank is measured in bench/defect_uq; the defaults keep R exact.

energy_reference is "absolute" (default: the model's energy, isolated-atom energies E0 included) or "E0": the energy relative to the isolated atoms, sum_i (E_i - E0[z_i]). With "E0" the per-atom constant (~-160 eV for Si) is never added to the site energies, so the total of a large cell stays small and keeps resolution: an energy-based line search (ASE PreconLBFGS's Armijo test) otherwise stops resolving energy decreases once they fall below the ulp of |E| ~ 160 eV x N, at fmax ~ 1e-4..1e-5 eV/A on 10^4-10^5 atoms (docs/dev/energy-sum-results.md). Forces and stress are unchanged. results["e0_offset"] is sum_i E0[z_i] (math.fsum; 0.0 for "absolute"), so the absolute energy is energy + e0_offset.

Memory: forces_std builds the force design rows of the WHOLE cell, about N3L*8 bytes (N atoms padded, L = (n_B + n_pair) * NZ columns) -- 7 GB for N = 100k at L = 3k -- on the JAX device, besides the posterior's L^2 factor. The edge Jacobian is node-chunked (linear_rows_chunked), the rows themselves are not: size cells to fit them. The rows come from the FULL model (never the energy-only eval_model), whatever lean is.

docs.title: eval_pair
docs.text:
eval_pair()

(model, meta) ready for direct evaluation -- the in-memory hand-off.

The four branch-selector meta keys are derived from the tree being handed over, exactly as export.save_npz does for the file path: the loader-side consumers (eval.io.load, and anything that reads meta to route branches) must never see authoring defaults that a patched tree has outgrown -- JAX clamps out-of-range branch indices silently, so a mismatch fails numerically, not loudly. The meta is deep-copied; the caller may mutate it freely. Structural checks guard the derivable keys (_resolve consumers read rcut/elements/n_* from meta).

ACECalculator(*auth.eval_pair()) and site_descriptors(auth.model, ..., meta=meta) evaluate the in-memory tree directly -- no npz round-trip; save_npz remains for ACEfit-fitted interchange and shell hand-off only.
